## **RESEARCH ARTICLE**

## **Desert Annual Plant Responses to Panel Microsites in a Low- Impact Utility- Scale Solar Energy Facility**

Claire C. Karban |  Seth M. Munson

U.S. Geological Survey, Southwest Biological Science Center, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA

**Correspondence:** Claire C. Karban (ckarban@usgs.gov)

**Received:** 5 June 2025 | **Revised:** 12 December 2025 | **Accepted:** 17 December 2025

## **Co- ordinating Editor:** Anaclara Guido

**Keywords:** disturbance | microclimate | Mojave Desert | plant diversity | renewable energy | single- axis photovoltaic panel | soil moisture | soil temperature | winter annual plant community

## **ABSTRACT**

**Aims:** Annual plants make up a large proportion of diversity in desert communities and are highly sensitive to changes in microclimate. The rapid development of utility- scale solar energy facilities throughout desert regions alters the local distribution of precipitation and shading, but the consequences for annual plant community composition and diversity are largely unknown. We evaluated the influence of single- axis tracking photovoltaic panels, and the microclimates they create, on annual plant communities in a utility- scale facility constructed with methods to minimize disturbance across three different vegetation–soil types. **Location:** The study was conducted in the eastern Mojave Desert, Nevada, USA.

**Methods:** We used 1- m[2] quadrats to sample annual plant density and diversity in 30 areas within the facility and 30 control areas outside the facility for each of three soil types characterized by distinct perennial vegetation. Each sampling area within the facility included three solar panel microsite categories: under panels, panel driplines, and between panels (interspace), which were compared to controls.

**Results:** We found that the effect of the microsites on native annual plant density and diversity depended on the vegetation–soil type. Solar panels increased native annual plant density and diversity in deep sandy soils but decreased density and diversity in shallow sandy soils. Annual plant diversity was higher in solar panel driplines compared to other microsites in a silty soil with low perennial cover. Microsite changes in shallow soil moisture resulted in differences in the annual plant community in deep soils, while soil surface temperature was a major influence in the shallow soil annual plant community.

**Conclusions:** Our results suggest that native annual plant diversity can increase with more heterogeneity in microclimate conditions created by low- impact photovoltaic facilities in arid settings, but effects depend on the underlying vegetation–soil type.

## **1   |   Introduction**

Annual plants represent up to half of plant diversity, stabilize soils, contribute to net primary production, and form the base of food webs in desert communities (Inouye 1991; Venable et al. 1993). Despite their importance and ubiquity, desert annuals are highly sensitive to both temporal and spatial variation in water availability and temperature compared to their

perennial counterparts (Mulroy and Rundel 1977). In wet years, their density and diversity can be very high, while in dry years, many annual plants escape drought by persisting in the soil seed bank (Bowers 1987; Inouye 1991). At local scales, annual plant germination and growth closely track changes in microclimate (Beatley 1974). Microclimatic fluctuations can be influenced by land- use change (Xian et al. 2020), and understanding how these land development- induced fluctuations

affect annual plant diversity can inform the resilience of desert ecosystems.

Utility- scale solar energy (USSE) facilities are a novel land- use rapidly expanding in desert ecosystems globally (International Energy Agency 2024). Traditional USSE site preparation and construction includes land grading and compaction, as well as topsoil and vegetation removal (Macknick et al. 2013). These traditional methods can alter soil properties and spread nonnative plants (Lovich and Ennen 2011; Hernandez et al. 2014; Choi et al. 2020), resulting in a landscape that does not support native plant diversity (e.g., Grodsky and Hernandez 2020). However, alternative site preparation and construction methods that limit disturbance can support both native vegetation and the generation of solar energy (Macknick et al. 2013; Moore- O'Leary et al. 2017; Sturchio and Knapp 2023; Karban et al. 2024). Minimizing soil surface grading and leaving undisturbed patches within solar panel arrays can maintain soil resources and native plant cover (Grodsky and Hernandez 2020; Karban et al. 2025). Additionally, adjusting the height and spacing of solar panels can influence the infrastructure's effects on abiotic factors and microclimate conditions (Wynne- Sison et al. 2023).

USSE facilities that utilize these less- destructive construction methods can create unique microclimates with implications for annual plant diversity. It is generally expected that plant diversity in arid systems should increase as environmental stress decreases (Odum and Barrett 2004), but the impact of solar facilities on microclimates, and thus environmental stress, is not yet clear. At the landscape scale, USSE facilities can increase nighttime air temperatures, both within and adjacent to the facility (Barron- Gafford et al. 2016; Devitt et al. 2022) and increase soil water and plant biomass (Liu et al. 2019). At a smaller scale, solar panels create novel microsites within the facilities by providing shade and redistributing precipitation, creating distinct microclimates. Solar panels moderate soil temperatures beneath their footprint—warming soils in the winter months and cooling them in the summer months (Liu et al. 2019; Yue et al. 2021; Wynne- Sison et al. 2023), which can result in higher soil moisture in shaded areas beneath panels (Yue et al. 2021; Sturchio et al. 2024). Microclimatic changes from experimental solar panel setups can increase soil seedbank survival (Hernandez et al. 2020) and impact annual plant diversity, with the direction of diversity effects dependent on precipitation amount and soil texture (Tanner et al. 2020).

In addition to microclimate, the community composition of desert annual plants can be influenced by the existing perennial vegetation and soil type in which they occur (Abella et al. 2023; Munson et al. 2015). Desert perennial plant species and their spatial distributions can influence soil fertility and nurse plant effects that encourage annual plant establishment (Abella et al. 2023). Different soil types vary in their texture, bulk density, depth, and water holding capacity—collectively influencing infiltration, retention, and availability of water for plant uptake (Munson et al. 2015). In an arid setting characterized by low precipitation and high potential evapotranspiration, we predict increased annual plant density and diversity in habitats (i.e., vegetation–soil types) and panel microsites that elevate shallow soil moisture.

In this study, we examined the effects of solar panels on native annual plant density and diversity in the Mojave Desert at a USSE facility that was constructed with alternative low- impact methods. Our study objectives were to answer two questions: (1) How do solar panel microsites influence native annual plant density, community composition, and diversity? And (2) are these annual plant responses affected by the underlying vegetation and soil type, disturbance, non- native plant cover, and microclimatic conditions?

## **2   |   Methods**

## **2.1   |   Site Description**

This study was conducted 50 km northeast of Las Vegas, Nevada, USA (36°28′N, 114°45′W) at the Gemini Solar photovoltaic (PV) facility (“Gemini”). The facility was constructed on 28 km[2] (Bureau of Land Management 2019a) and has a capacity of 690 MW alternating current provided by bifacial, single- axis tracking panels, with 380 MW 4- h battery energy storage. The site is in the Mojave Desert, with a mean annual precipitation of 165 mm falling primarily in the winter and spring. Average annual high and low temperatures are 27.1°C and 14.4°C, respectively (Western Regional Climate Center 2023). The Mojave Desert plant communities are made up of persistent shrublands, with annual plants contributing a large ephemeral source of diversity during years with favorable precipitation. Ninety- three percent of the study area is creosote bush ( _Larrea tridentata_ )— white bursage ( _Ambrosia dumosa_ ) shrubland, occurring on both young, deep, sandy soils (Arada and Tonopah soil series) and older, shallow sandy soils (Bard and Mormon Mesa soil series) with an underlying petrocalcic horizon at 20–30 cm beneath the soil surface (Phoenix Biological Consulting 2018). Approximately 5% of the project area is defined as saltbush ( _Atriplex_ spp.) shrubland, occurring on fine, silty soils (Spring silty clay loam soil series; Phoenix Biological Consulting 2018). In this study, soil texture and depth and the shrub component of plant communities were used to divide the sampling area into three vegetation–soil types: deep sandy creosote bush (“deep creosote bush”), shallow sandy creosote bush (“shallow creosote bush”), and silty saltbush (Appendix S1).

Site preparation at the Gemini facility, including the establishment of roads and fences, occurred in 2021. Site construction occurred in 2022 and 2023. Site preparation and construction methods at Gemini were intended to create a solar facility that can co- function as habitat (Karban et al. 2024). Construction was limited to discrete areas as needed to install solar panel arrays. In these areas, vegetation and soils were driven over and crushed with limited vehicle passes, and vegetation under panels was trimmed to a height of 45–60 cm to limit interference with panels (Bureau of Land Management 2019a). Panel rows were located approximately 8.75 m apart from one another, measuring from panel center to panel center, and solar panels were 2.4 m wide. Solar panel energization was still being tested throughout the sampling period (late April 2024), resulting in inconsistent east–west rotation of the panels before and during the sampling period. The facility permit required that non- native species within Gemini be kept at or below control site cover levels and Sahara mustard ( _Brassica_

_tournefortii_ ) be fully removed from rare plant habitats (Bureau of Land Management 2019b) using a combination of mechanical removal and glyphosate application.

## **2.2   |   Sample Design and Data Collection**

The Mojave Desert supports primarily winter annual species, which germinate in late fall or early winter and conduct most of their growth in the spring (Beatley 1974). Therefore, data were collected in April 2024 following a wetter- than- average September 2023, drier- than- average October to December 2023, and above- average precipitation in January to March 2024 (Appendix S2). To answer the research questions, sixty 100 m transects were established—30 within the Gemini facility solar arrays and 30 in nearby undeveloped control areas with similar environmental characteristics (Figure 1). The west endpoint of each transect was randomly placed within each vegetation–soil type and extended to the east,

perpendicular to the rows of solar panels if in the facility. In April 2024, three areas along each transect were sampled (Figure 1). Each sampling area included three microsite categories that were each sampled with a 2 m × 0.5 m quadrat: Interspace (IS) was centered between solar panels, east and west driplines (DL) were centered on the east and west edges of solar panels when panels were horizontal, and under panel (UP) was centered directly beneath the solar panel (Figure 1 inset). The east and west driplines were lumped together into one category—“DL” to deal with inconsistencies in panel position and rotation before and during the sampling period. The short end of the quadrat (0.5 m) was placed at a tangent to the north edge of the transect so that the long edge of the quadrat (2 m) ran parallel to the solar panel row. In each quadrat, the number of individuals of each annual plant species was recorded. To minimize bias, individual plants that occurred under the north or east quadrat frame edge were counted “in” the quadrat and individual plants that overlapped the south or west quadrat boundary were considered “out” of the

Meteorological stations are where abiotic microsite data were collected. quadrat. Each 1- m[2] quadrat was subdivided into one hundred 10 cm × 10 cm squares (each square = 1% of the total quadrat area) by colored string to facilitate ocular estimation of canopy cover by species in each quadrat. The field crew trained and calibrated on ocular estimation of cover, and observer bias for measurements was checked during data collection. Appendix S3 includes all annual plant species that were recorded during sampling. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Plants Database (https:// plants. usda. gov) was used to classify plant species’ origins as “native” or “non- native.” Non- native annual plant cover was calculated as the sum of all non- native species percent canopy cover in each quadrat. Disturbance was recorded as the proportion of each southernmost 0.5- m quadrat edge that was intercepted by visible human alterations to soil or vegetation related to facility construction or maintenance, such as human footprints and, primarily, vehicle tracks. The starting point and ending point of any disturbance that intersected the quadrat edge were recorded and used to calculate the percentage of each quadrat edge that was disturbed.

Microclimate measurements were collected at meteorological stations coupled with sensor arrays in the shallow and deep creosote bush (but not silty saltbush due to logistical constraints) vegetation–soil types from September 15, 2023, to April 30, 2024 (Pinos et al. 2026). There were two stations per microsite per vegetation–soil type (Figure 1), which collected measurements of soil surface temperature (SI- 111SS, infrared radiometer, Apogee Instruments), air temperature and relative humidity 0.5 m above the soil surface (EE181- L probe, Campbell Scientific), soil temperature 0–15 cm belowground (TCAV- L soil thermocouple Probe, Campbell Scientific), soil moisture at 10 cm belowground and 40 cm belowground (TEROS 10 and TEROS 11 sensors, METER Group), and photosynthetically active radiation 0.5 m above the soil surface (CS310 quantum PAR sensor, Apogee Instruments). Variables were logged every 1 min (Model CR1000X, Campbell Scientific) and aggregated at 15 min and then averaged by day. Daily microclimate averages were further summarized by the entire sampling period, or by season (fall: September 15, 2023, to December 15, 2023, winter: December 16, 2023, to March 15, 2024, and spring: March 16, 2024, to April 30, 2024) given the importance of seasonal variations for annual plant germination and growth (Beatley 1974). Correlations between these seasonal variables were analyzed, and variables were excluded based on collinearity. For example, photosynthetically active radiation was considered as a potential variable, but it was excluded because it was highly correlated with soil surface temperature and air temperature—both of which were included in the analysis. The final microclimate variables selected for model inclusion were winter mean soil surface temperature, winter maximum soil surface temperature, spring mean soil surface temperature, spring maximum soil surface temperature, mean air temperature, mean volumetric water content at 10 cm, and mean volumetric water content at 40 cm.

## **2.3   |   Calculations**

Plant density (total number of individual plants per m[2] ) and species richness (total number of species per m[2] ) were calculated within each quadrat. The Shannon–Wiener diversity index

(hereafter “Shannon diversity”) was calculated based on species richness and the evenness of the abundance of species within each quadrat (Appendix S4). Pielou's evenness (hereafter “evenness”) was calculated as a way to describe the distribution of species abundance in the community, where an evenness value of 1 means all species have the same abundance (Appendix S4).

Relative species abundance was predicted to be more sensitive to changes in resource alterations than other common metrics of community change (Collins et al. 2008). To examine how solar panel microclimates influenced relative abundance in the native annual plant communities, rank abundance curves were generated for each vegetation–soil type using abundance data for all native annual species. Differences in species’ ranks (rank difference, i.e., reordering) and compositions (i.e., species substitution) between microsites were identified using the “RAC_ difference” function in the codyn R package (Hallett et al. 2020; Appendix S4). Rank difference is bound between 0 at the low end and 0.5 as the maximum rank change possible.

## **2.4   |   Statistical Analyses**

To determine how solar panel microsites and underlying site conditions influenced native annual plant density and diversity, a series of zero- inflated linear mixed models were fitted. Zero- inflated models treat zeros as a mixture of structural and sampling zeros, modeling them accordingly with a mixture of a Bernoulli distribution and another distribution (in this case Gaussian or lognormal). First, “full models” that included vegetation–soil type, microsite, disturbance, and non- native cover as explanatory variables were fitted. The sampling area nested within the transect was included as a random effect. Disturbance and non- native cover variables were standardized with a mean of zero and standard deviation of 1 to enable easier comparison of effect sizes. Annual plant density and diversity had distinct patterns in each vegetation–soil type, indicated by significant pairwise differences in post hoc testing, so each vegetation–soil type was modeled separately. These model results were used to examine how each diversity metric was affected by the solar panel microsites, after controlling for any influences of disturbance and non- native cover. Models were fit using either a Gaussian distribution (for Shannon diversity) or a lognormal distribution (for density, richness, and evenness) in the R package glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017). Model fit was assessed by examining model residuals in the DHARMa R package (Hartig 2022). The relative strength of predictors was compared with a Wald type II chisquared test using the “Anova” function in the car R package (Fox and Weisberg 2018). Post hoc pairwise comparisons were made in the emmeans R package (Lenth 2023). When non- native cover or disturbance were significant predictors of diversity or density in these models, another round of linear mixed- effects models were fit with density or diversity as the response variable, and disturbance and non- native cover as interactive main effects. The sampling area nested within the transect was included as a random effect. For these models, a separate model was fit for each microsite within each vegetation–soil type to separate the effects of non- native cover and disturbance from microsite effects. Model fit was assessed by examining model residuals in the DHARMa R package (Hartig 2022). Post hoc pairwise comparisons were made in the emmeans R package (Lenth 2023).

To understand how vegetation–soil type and microclimate influence annual plant communities, nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) was done using a Bray–Curtis dissimilarity matrix on native annual plant relative abundance data. Each vegetation–soil type was analyzed separately, and the number of dimensions for each type was chosen by plotting 1–10 dimensions and selecting the lowest number of dimensions that minimized stress (4 for deep creosote bush and silty saltbush and 3 for shallow creosote bush). A PERMANOVA from the “adonis” function in the vegan package (Oksanen et al. 2022) was used on the relative abundances of species in each microsite to assess whether the means of centroids from each microsite were statistically different. Differences between microsites were evaluated using the “pairwise.adonis” function (Martinez Arbizu 2020). Significant differences between microsites can be caused by spatial patterning in the dispersion of points, which was assessed using the “betadisper” function in the vegan package (Oksanen et al. 2022). Finally, environmental data were mapped as vectors onto each NMDS ordination space using the “envfit” function in the vegan package to determine correlations between environmental variables and microsites. The mapped output provides the direction cosines for each environmental vector in ordination space, and the length of each vector is scaled by the strength of its correlation (Oksanen et al. 2022).

## **3   |   Results**

## **3.1   |   Annual Plant Density and Diversity**

Solar panel microsites were the primary driver of native annual plant density and diversity (Appendix S5), but the effects varied by vegetation–soil type and the density or diversity response metric (Appendix S6).

Native annual plant density was higher in interspaces and panel driplines compared to controls in deep creosote bush (Figure 2A; Appendix S7). In contrast, density decreased as panel influence increased in the shallow creosote bush, with the lowest density beneath solar panels. In the silty saltbush vegetation–soil type, none of the panel microsites differed in density compared to the controls, but density was higher in panel interspaces than beneath panels.

In deep creosote bush, species richness was 5.4 (±0.4) in interspaces and 4.8 (±0.4) in panel driplines, nearly double the richness of 2.8 (±0.3) in the controls, while richness directly under the panels was similar to controls (Figure 2B; Appendix S7). In the shallow creosote bush control quadrats, species richness was 7.3 (±0.6) and not significantly different than interspaces,

but driplines (5.2 ± 0.4) had significantly lower richness, as did under panel microsites (3.8 ± 0.5) (Figure 2B; Appendix S7). Species richness did not vary significantly by microsite in silty saltbush.

The Shannon diversity index followed similar patterns to species richness. Diversity was higher in panel driplines and panel interspaces in the facility compared to off- site controls in deep creosote bush, while diversity directly under the panels was similar to that of the controls (Figure 2C; Appendix S7). Diversity was lower under solar panels compared to controls in shallow creosote bush but was not significantly different from controls in driplines and panel interspaces (Figure 2C; Appendix S7). Diversity was higher in panel driplines compared to controls in silty saltbush (Figure 2C; Appendix S7).

Evenness was lower in panel interspaces in the facility compared to off- site controls in deep creosote bush, while evenness in panel driplines and directly under the panels was similar to that at controls (Figure 2D; Appendix S7). Evenness was higher in all solar panel microsites compared to controls in shallow creosote bush (Figure 2D; Appendix S7). Evenness was higher in driplines and under panels compared to controls in silty saltbush, while panel interspaces did not differ significantly from controls (Figure 2D; Appendix S7).

## **3.2   |   Community Composition and Microclimate**

Community composition was significantly influenced by microsite in each of the vegetation–soil types (Figure 3; Appendix S8).

In the deep creosote bush, all facility microsites were significantly different from control areas (Figure 3A; Appendix S9). Dispersion, the variance within each microsite, was significantly lower for the dripline and interspace communities compared to the control community (Figure 3A; Appendix S10). Community composition divergence was partially explained by species rank differences (Appendix S11). _Pectocarya heterocarpa_ and _P. platycarpa_ , which were the two most dominant species in control communities, shifted to subdominant positions in the dripline and interspace communities (Figure 3D). In their places, _Eriophyllum lanosum_ was a dominant species in all microsites within the facility, but not in control areas, and _Chaenactis carphoclinia_ was a dominant species in driplines and interspaces, but not in control areas. There were also a higher number of rare plant species in the panel dripline and interspace communities compared to the controls. Differences in the native annual plant communities within the facility were correlated with altered microclimates, including higher mean air temperature, higher maximum winter soil surface temperature, and higher mean soil moisture at 10 cm depth (Appendix S12) compared to control microsites (Figure 3A; Appendix S13).

In the shallow creosote bush, native annual plant community composition at microsites within the facility was significantly different from the controls (Figure 3B; Appendix S9). Within the facility, the community composition under panels and in panel interspaces also differed significantly. Dispersion was higher in the dripline and under panel communities compared to controls (Appendix S10). Despite these differences, species reordering and replacement were low in shallow creosote bush and did not explain differences in community composition (Figure 3E; Appendix S11). Instead, community composition differences between inside and outside of the facility and under panels and compared to panel interspaces were related to spring mean soil surface temperature, spring maximum soil surface temperature, mean air temperature (Figure 3B; Appendix S13) – variables that are related to panel shading. Driplines and panel interspaces were also correlated with lower soil moisture at 40 cm depth but slightly higher soil moisture at 10 cm depth (Figure 3B; Appendix S13).

In the silty saltbush, the native annual plant community composition under panels was significantly different from the controls

(Figure 3C; Appendix S9). Dispersion did not differ among any microsites (Appendix S8). However, there were fewer rare species under panel microsites compared to the controls, and there were differences in species and the rank order in which they occurred in the community, likely explaining divergence between these communities (Appendix S11). In particular, _Festuca octoflora_ and _Eriogonum deflexum_ , the third and fourth most dominant species in the control areas, were less common and absent, respectively, from the under panel microsites (Figure 3F). _Pectocarya heterocarpa_ and _P. platycarpa_ were both dominant within facility microsites but not in the control areas.

## **3.3   |   Disturbance and Non- Native Annuals**

Both non- native species cover (Figure 4A) and disturbance (Figure 4B) varied by panel microsites. Non- native plant cover was higher in driplines than controls for all vegetation–soil types, and it was lower under panels in deep creosote bush and silty saltbush (Figure 4A). While the microsite was a more important driver of native annual plant density and diversity in other soil types, non- native cover more strongly predicted native annual plant density and Shannon diversity in silty saltbush (Appendix S5). This was driven by positive correlations between non- native cover and native annual abundance and diversity in the controls, driplines, and panel interspaces. There were negative correlations between non- native cover and diversity beneath panels (Appendices S14 and S15), while non- native cover was positively correlated with evenness under panels in deep creosote bush (Appendix S16).

The level of disturbance was higher in the interspaces than under panels for shallow creosote bush and trended the same way in deep creosote bush, while driplines had an intermediate level of disturbance (Figure 4B). Silty saltbush had higher under panel disturbance compared to driplines (Figure 4B). Disturbance was negatively correlated with native annual plant density in shallow creosote bush interspaces (Appendix S14). There was a significant main effect of disturbance on Shannon diversity in silty saltbush—the only positive effect of disturbance on any diversity metrics that were analyzed (Appendix S15).

## **4   |   Discussion**

## **4.1   |   Solar Panel Microsite Effects on Density and Diversity Depend on Vegetation–Soil Type**

We found that solar panel microsites influenced native annual plant density and diversity, but the direction of the effect varied by vegetation–soil type and response metric. Because water availability is the driving force behind many vegetation patterns in dryland ecosystems (Munson et al. 2015), variability in soil moisture among vegetation–soil types and microsites likely influenced the annual plant communities in our study. The deep, coarse- textured soils in the deep creosote bush vegetation–soil type may support low annual plant abundance and richness because soil moisture can quickly drain out of the annual plant rooting zone. In these soils, shading provided by solar panels in the facility may have prolonged soil moisture at shallow depths, evidenced by higher plant density and richness in panel interspaces that were affected by shade. Areas located beneath panels did not appear to confer the same benefit, possibly because light reduction was too pronounced. Soil surface temperature was also warmer within the facility in the deep creosote soils, particularly during the winter months. The combination of increased moisture and warmer soils may have promoted seed germination (Beatley 1974), increasing native annual plant density and diversity. Our results suggest that benefits to annual diversity from shade may be limited to conditions that are strongly water- limited, as in the deep creosote soils. This finding is in line with other research showing the greatest benefits of solar panel shade to the annual plant community in more stressful habitat during dry years in the Mojave Desert (Tanner et al. 2020). In the Sonoran Desert, shaded microclimates created by solar panels increased annual plant richness (Patten and Smith 1980; Smith et al. 1987), and Shannon diversity was higher in shaded microclimates in a Mediterranean climate (Li et al. 2025). Our findings also more broadly support the hypothesis that plant diversity in arid systems should increase as environmental stress decreases (Odum and Barrett 2004).

In contrast, solar panels decreased annual plant density and richness in the shallow creosote bush. This vegetation–soil type had higher soil moisture in the shallow rooting zone of annual plants compared to the deep creosote bush, likely due to the perching of water above the petrocalcic horizon (Herbel et al. 1972; Duniway et al. 2010). This moisture enabled the control shallow creosote bush sites to support high species richness and diversity compared to the other vegetation–soil types. The controls in the vegetation–soil type also had higher surface temperatures compared to those within the facility. In this more diverse vegetation–soil type, the reduction of density and diversity within the facility could be a signal of the physical disturbance from facility construction, as annual plant density was negatively related to increasing disturbance. Studies conducted in wetter grassland systems have also found lower plant diversity in solar panel arrays (Armstrong et al. 2016; Vervloesem et al. 2022), which, together with our results, suggests that panel microclimate effects on annual plant diversity may switch from positive to negative as water becomes less limiting. Species evenness in shallow creosote bush increased in the facility, particularly in the driplines and under panels where density and richness declined. This suggests that community changes may have been

driven by panel microsite changes in surface temperature and soil moisture, which may influence germination of dominant annual plants and change their relative abundances within the community.

The silty saltbush sites likely supported low annual plant diversity and richness because the soils are very sodic, which can influence germination and water balance of the developing plants (reviewed in Hailu and Mehari 2021). Higher Shannon diversity in the dripline at the silty saltbush sites may be attributable to increased soil moisture due to runoff from the panels. Additionally, perennial plant cover is lowest in this soil type (Karban et al. 2025). In the absence of shrubs to provide nurse effects, it is possible that the shading and increased moisture available in the panel driplines were more important for annual plant germination and growth compared to other vegetation– soil types.

Despite the mixed effects of panels on native annual diversity across vegetation–soil types, the total facility area with increased diversity was greater than the area with decreased diversity. The size and layout of the solar panel arrays across the entire facility are such that about 12% of the array area was located directly beneath panels, 24% was located below driplines, and the remaining 64% of the array area was located interspace. Shallow creosote bush accounted for the largest vegetation–soil type in the facility at 13.94 km[2] , followed by deep creosote bush at 10.83 km[2] , and silty saltbush at 3.14 km[2] . Weighting the diversity changes by each microsite and vegetation–soil type area reveals that only about 1.67 km[2] , or 6%, of the total facility area likely experienced a decline in Shannon diversity (under panel microsites in shallow creosote), and about 5.02 km[2] , or 18%, of the total facility area showed a decline in native annual species richness (under panel and dripline microsites in shallow creosote). Our sampling design did not capture variables on a continuum of distance from panel or species–area relationships, but these facility- wide estimates indicate that the majority of the facility experienced either no significant changes or increases in diversity.

## **4.2   |   Community Composition Is Driven by Microclimatic Changes and Species Reordering**

In deep creosote bush, our results suggest that increased shallow soil moisture from solar panel shading in the interspace, and shading and panel runoff to driplines, altered annual plant community composition. These deep, sandy soils typically do not retain much shallow moisture in arid settings, and so the increase in shallow moisture within the facility may have increased available niche space for annual plants in this vegetation–soil type. In shallow creosote bush, higher mean winter soil surface temperature and lower mean and maximum springtime soil surface temperatures under panels and in panel driplines may prolong periods favorable for germination and growth, similarly increasing niche space. In our study, soil surface temperature was highly correlated with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), so it is likely that the effect of lower temperatures in shaded microsites is related to decreases in PAR. At Gemini, microsites directly under panels received 22% of the PAR compared to controls outside the facility, and driplines received 49%

of the PAR of controls. These reductions are smaller than other published work that has emphasized the role of reduced PAR as a driver of plant community changes (e.g., Li et al. 2025) in part because the spacing between panels at Gemini is larger.

Within deep creosote bush and silty saltbush, there were more species substitutions and reorderings across microsites than in shallow creosote bush. In deep creosote bush, _Eriophyllum lanosum_ and _Chaenactis carphoclinia_ were dominant species within the facility but not in the control areas. Like many winter annual species, _E. lanosum_ is known to bet hedge, responding to a variety of complex combinations of germination cues (Adondakis and Venable 2004; Gremer et al. 2016). Bet- hedging strategies succeed in variable environments, and the increased heterogeneity created by the solar panels may benefit species that bet hedge across different environmental conditions. _Chaenactis carphoclinia_ has been described as shrub- dependent (Muller 1953), suggesting that it benefits from the microclimatic conditions that shrubs provide, which may be partially replicated by the shade of solar panels. In the silty saltbush soils, _Pectocarya heterocarpa_ —dominant in the facility but not in the controls—is known to use seed heteromorphism as a bet- hedging strategy (Adondakis and Venable 2004), which, again, may be advantageous under the increased heterogeneity created by solar panels. _Festuca octoflora_ was dominant in controls but not within the facility, in line with its common occurrence in open, sunny habitats or after fire (Howard 2006). The native forbs associated with the solar facility provide more nutritional forage than _F. octoflora_ for wildlife species of conservation concern such as the desert tortoise (Drake et al. 2016). It should be noted that these species- level differences are correlational, and our study design cannot rule out the possibility that the differences existed prior to the construction of the solar facility.

## **4.3   |   Influence of Non- Native Plant Cover and Disturbance**

moisture. The ongoing vegetation management at the Gemini facility includes active removal of non- native species through herbicide application and hand pulling, which may have led to low densities that did not negatively affect native diversity in the facility. Given that our study took place 1 year after construction, many non- native species may not have had sufficient time to proliferate across the facility to negatively affect the native annual community.

Our short- term results suggest that solar panel microsites, and the novel microclimates they create, can shape the trajectory of native annual plant communities in an arid, USSE solar facility constructed using low- impact methods. Desert native annual plant communities can benefit in microsites that alleviate water limitation, particularly under more environmentally stressful conditions. Non- native species may provide a secondary influence on native annual plant communities, particularly if they proliferate over the long term.

## **Conflicts of Interest**

The construction methods used at Gemini explain disturbance patterns in the facility. Vehicles drove up and down the interspaces to install infrastructure, resulting in higher disturbance in those microsites. Higher disturbance under panels in the silty saltbush vegetation–soil types may be attributable to higher vehicular activity in that area. Disturbance was not a significant driver of native annual density and diversity in most cases, in line with previous research that finds that effects of precipitation can be larger than effects of disturbance (from fire, in this case) when looking at annual plant succession in deserts (reviewed in Abella 2010). Our findings also suggest that the low- impact methods used during facility construction led to the provisioning of native annual diversity. In contrast, intensive removal of vegetation and soil surface layers in traditionally constructed facilities, can reduce nearly all annual plants (Grodsky and Hernandez 2020).

Non- native plant cover was higher in driplines, where higher moisture may favor competitive non- native species (Brooks and Berry 2006). Non- native plant cover was a slightly more important factor and was significantly positively correlated with Shannon diversity and abundance in some vegetation–soil types.
